task: Compare how two works you have studied present the relationship between an individual's sense of identity and the social roles imposed on that individual.
text:
Both Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House and Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis place a young woman inside a society that has already decided what she is for, and then follow her as she works out who she is. Yet the two writers disagree about where that identity is won and what it costs. Ibsen, working in the closed form of a realist drawing-room play, shows identity discovered in a single violent act of refusal, whereas Satrapi, using the open and episodic form of an autobiographical graphic novel, shows it assembled slowly through mistakes, exile and return. I will argue that both works expose the social role as a performance, but that Ibsen treats the performance as something that must be abandoned entirely, while Satrapi suggests that a self can survive by performing consciously and on its own terms.

In A Doll's House the social role is built into the language the characters use to each other. Torvald never addresses Nora as an equal; he calls her his little skylark and his squirrel, and these diminutives turn her into an animal that sings and scampers when it is wanted and is scolded when it spends too much. Ibsen's choice of pets rather than, say, servants is revealing, because it shows a control that is affectionate on the surface and therefore hard to resist. Nora collaborates in it. She hides macaroons, tells small lies about money, and plays the extravagant, silly wife because that is the version of herself that earns Torvald's approval. The tarantella she dances at the party is the play's central image of this performance: she rehearses wildly, tears at her shawl, and dances as though her life depended on it, which in fact it does, since Torvald is about to read Krogstad's letter. The dance is a public display of private panic, and Ibsen lets the audience see both at once. What Nora presents as charm is really a woman performing happiness to protect a secret, her forging of her father's signature to pay for the trip that saved her husband's life. Her identity is divided between the role she shows and the act of real courage she hides, and the tragedy is that the society around her would recognise only the second as a crime.

Satrapi also shows identity being dictated from outside, but the dictation is political and religious rather than domestic. After the Revolution the veil becomes compulsory, and the opening chapter, titled The Veil, shows the ten-year-old Marji and her classmates using their headscarves as skipping ropes and monster masks, treating a symbol of state power as a toy. The black and white drawing matters here. Because there is no colour, the veil, the guardians of the revolution and the schoolgirls are all built from the same heavy black shapes, so the children's play visibly resists the regime's attempt to make those shapes mean something solemn. Later, when Marji is a teenager, performance becomes a skill for survival. She learns to look pious in public, to hide her punk jacket and her Iron Maiden tape, and to produce tears and a convincing story when the guardians stop her in the street. Just as Nora flatters Torvald with a role, Marji gives the regime a role, the docile girl, and keeps her real self behind it. The crucial difference is that Marji knows she is acting. Her narration looks back at her younger self from a mature distance, which makes the performance an object of irony rather than of shame.

Ibsen compresses the discovery of the self into three acts in one room. The tight construction, in which every hidden thing is pulled into the light by the arrival of Krogstad's letter, makes Nora's transformation feel inevitable rather than sudden. The turning point comes not when the secret is exposed but a moment later, when Torvald's first reaction is to call her a hypocrite and a criminal, concerned only for his name, and then, once the danger has passed, to forgive her as though nothing had happened. It is that second reversal which shows Nora that the love she believed in was also a role. Her final speech is calm, almost like a business meeting, and the plain prose contrasts deliberately with the hysteria of the tarantella. She says that she has passed from her father's hands to her husband's and has never been a human being first. The door that slams at the end is the dramatic equivalent of a full stop. Ibsen gives the audience no sequel, so the freedom is total and also unguaranteed, and part of the play's force lies in the way the audience must live with what it cannot see.

Satrapi's structure is the opposite. Persepolis does not hurry; it follows Marji across about fourteen years and through several versions of herself: the child who wants to be a prophet, the teenage punk in Tehran, the lonely student in Vienna, the depressed young woman who comes home and tries to fit in again. At each stage she makes a choice that is partly a failure. In Vienna, asked where she comes from, she says she is French, a lie that makes her feel light for an instant and then exposes the very thing she is trying to escape. These episodes work because Satrapi lets the older narrator judge the younger Marji without excusing her. Her grandmother's advice to keep her dignity and be true to herself runs through the book as a conscience, a standard inherited from a woman she loves rather than imposed by a husband or a state. Where Nora finds herself in a decision to leave, Marji finds herself in a pattern of leaving and returning, falling and recovering. Ibsen's single door becomes Satrapi's repeated airports.

It would be too neat, however, to say that both heroines simply find themselves. Nora's freedom is ambiguous. She has no money, no profession and, by her own admission, no real education, and she walks out on her children, which Ibsen refuses to present as an easy choice: the tone of the last scene is sorrow as much as triumph. Satrapi's account of freedom is also complicated, by class. Marji's family are educated, secular and well-off enough to send her to Europe, an escape unavailable to the maid Mehri, whose love affair ends in humiliation early in the book, and Satrapi is aware of this, drawing her own privilege into the narrative rather than hiding it. In both works, then, the individual's liberty depends on resources that the society has not given everyone.

The works differ finally in what they take the enemy of identity to be. For Ibsen it is an intimate, almost invisible habit of condescension, and the form of the play, a single room that could be any bourgeois home, makes the problem general. For Satrapi it is an ideology enforced by the state, but she is equally critical of the West that receives her in Vienna with indifference, so that no society is allowed to be the answer. Both authors conclude that identity cannot be handed over by a role, whether it is called wife or believer, and both leave their heroines alone at the end. The meaning each makes of that aloneness is where they part: Ibsen presents it as the price of being a person, and Satrapi as the condition from which a person can finally choose to belong.

task: How do two works you have studied present the pursuit of a dream and its consequences for the individual?
text:
The pursuit of a dream is an important theme in many works of literature and in both The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald and Death of a Salesman by Arthur Miller the main character chases the American Dream and it leads to their downfall. In this essay I am going to compare how the two writers present this theme and what the consequences are for Jay Gatsby and Willy Loman. I will look at characterisation, symbolism and structure in each work and then compare them.

The Great Gatsby is narrated by Nick Carraway, who moves to West Egg in the summer of 1922 and becomes the neighbour of Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire who throws enormous parties every weekend. Nick later finds out that Gatsby throws the parties because he hopes that Daisy Buchanan, the woman he loved before the war, will come to one of them. Daisy is Nick's cousin and she lives across the bay in East Egg with her husband Tom, who is very rich and has a mistress called Myrtle Wilson. Gatsby tells Nick his story and Nick arranges a meeting at his own house. Gatsby and Daisy begin an affair. Gatsby shows Daisy his mansion and his shirts, and she cries because she has never seen such beautiful shirts. Later in the summer there is a confrontation in a hotel in New York where Tom tells Daisy that Gatsby is a bootlegger and a criminal. On the way home Daisy is driving Gatsby's car and she kills Myrtle, but Gatsby says he will take the blame. George Wilson thinks Gatsby was Myrtle's lover and shoots him in his swimming pool. Almost nobody comes to the funeral except Nick and Gatsby's father.

The main symbol in the novel is the green light at the end of Daisy's dock, which Gatsby looks at across the water. This represents his dream because it is far away and he cannot reach it. Fitzgerald uses colour symbolism a lot, for example green for hope and money, and yellow and white for Daisy, who is described as having a voice full of money. The Valley of Ashes is another symbol, which shows the poor people who are left behind by the American Dream, and the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg on the billboard watch over everything like God. These symbols show that the dream is false because the rich people are careless and carelessness is what destroys the dreamers. Nick says that Tom and Daisy were careless people who smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money. This shows that Gatsby's dream was corrupted from the beginning.

Death of a Salesman is a play which is about Willy Loman, a travelling salesman of sixty-three who is losing his job and his mind. The play happens over twenty-four hours in his house in Brooklyn but there are also many flashbacks to the past where Willy remembers his sons Biff and Happy when they were young, and his brother Ben who went to Africa and became rich. Willy believes that being well liked is the key to success and he teaches this to his sons. Biff was a football star but he failed maths and did not go to college, and he found out that Willy was having an affair with a woman in Boston, which ruined their relationship. In the present, Willy is fired by his boss Howard after asking for a job in New York. Biff tries to get a business loan from his old employer but he steals a pen and leaves. In the end Willy decides to kill himself in a car crash so that his family will get the insurance money, and at the requiem only a few people attend the funeral. Linda, his wife, says that she cannot cry and that she made the last payment on the house.

Miller uses the structure of the play to show Willy's dream. The flashbacks are shown by changes in the lighting and the music, for example the sound of a flute that is associated with Willy's father, and this shows that Willy is living in the past and cannot face the present. The set is a cut-away house with the apartment buildings looming over it, which shows that Willy is trapped and that the city is closing in on him. The title Death of a Salesman also tells the audience from the beginning that he will die, so it is a tragedy, and Miller wrote an essay saying that the common man can be a tragic hero. The dialogue also shows his character because Willy contradicts himself often, saying that Biff is a lazy bum and then that he is going to be a great man a minute later.

There are several similarities between the two works. Firstly, both Gatsby and Willy have a dream which is based on money and success and both of them die at the end because of it. Secondly, both works use symbols to show that the dream is an illusion. In Gatsby it is the green light and in Death of a Salesman it is the seeds Willy tries to plant in the garden at night, which shows that he wants to leave something behind but nothing will grow in the shade of the buildings. Thirdly, both works are about the 1920s or just after it and are critical of capitalism. Both authors show that the American Dream is not available to everybody and that people who try to reach it are destroyed.

Another character who is important in both works is a friend who offers a different life. In Death of a Salesman Willy's neighbour Charley offers him a job again and again but Willy is too proud to accept it, and he says that Charley is not liked, even though Charley is the only person who really helps him. At the end Charley says at the requiem that nobody dares to blame this man, because a salesman has to dream. In The Great Gatsby the person who stays loyal is Nick, who tells Gatsby that he is worth the whole damn bunch put together, and he is the one who arranges the funeral. This shows that both writers think that real friendship is more important than the dream, but that the dreamers do not see it until it is too late. It also shows that both works are in a way about loneliness, because the main characters die with almost nobody there.

There are also some differences. Gatsby's dream is about love as well as money, because he wants Daisy, but Willy's dream is about success and being liked and about his sons. Also The Great Gatsby is a novel with a narrator, Nick, so we see Gatsby from the outside, whereas in Death of a Salesman we see Willy from the inside because the play shows his memories and his thoughts. Another difference is that Gatsby is a self-made man who started off poor as James Gatz and Willy is not self-made at all because he never really gets anywhere. Gatsby dies young but Willy is old.

In conclusion, both Fitzgerald and Miller present the pursuit of a dream as something that has bad consequences for the individual. They do this through symbols, characterisation and structure. Gatsby and Willy are both destroyed by their dream and the works show that the American Dream is an illusion. Although the two works are different in form, one is a novel and one is a play, they have a similar message about the dangers of the American Dream and the writers are critical of society. This is why they are still read today by many people.

task: Compare how two works you have studied explore loyalty and betrayal in human relationships.
text:
In this essay I will be comparing Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck and The Kite Runner by Khaled Hosseini. Both of these books are about loyalty and betrayal and they both have friendship in them. I think that Steinbeck and Hosseini show loyalty and betrayal in a lot of ways.

Of Mice and Men is about two men called George and Lennie who travel around California during the Great Depression looking for work on ranches. George is small and clever and Lennie is big and strong but he is not very smart and he likes to touch soft things like mice and puppies and this gets him into trouble. They have a dream that they will have their own farm one day and Lennie will tend the rabbits. They get a job on a ranch but the boss's son Curley is mean and has a wife who flirts with the men. Lennie accidentally kills Curley's wife while touching her hair and then he runs away to the place by the river that George told him to go to. In the end George shoots Lennie in the back of the head so that Curley and the others will not hurt him. This shows that George was loyal to Lennie because he did not want him to suffer. Steinbeck wrote the story in a very simple way and this makes it sad.

The Kite Runner is about Amir who is a boy in Afghanistan and his servant and friend Hassan who is a Hazara. Amir is jealous of Hassan because Baba his father loves Hassan too, and Hassan is very loyal and will do anything for Amir, he says for you a thousand times over. In the kite tournament Amir wins, and Hassan runs the kite for him but he is cornered by a bully called Assef and is raped, and Amir watches and does nothing because he is a coward. This is the betrayal. After that Amir feels guilty so he tries to get Hassan sent away by saying that he stole a watch. Hassan says that he did it, even though he did not. Years later Amir goes back to Afghanistan to rescue Hassan's son Sohrab from the Taliban and he finds out that Hassan was his half brother. This is Amir's way of making up for what he did.

Both of the books have a loyal friend and a betrayal. In Of Mice and Men George is loyal to Lennie and in the Kite Runner Hassan is loyal to Amir. Another similarity is that both books have a character who dies at the end, Lennie and Hassan, and the person who is left behind feels sad. Steinbeck and Hosseini also use symbols. In Of Mice and Men the rabbits is a symbol of the dream and in The Kite Runner the kite is a symbol of freedom and friendship. They also both use foreshadowing for example in Of Mice and Men Candy's dog is shot before the ending which foreshadows that Lennie will be shot. Hosseini uses flashbacks as well because the book is told by Amir when he is older.

There are some differences though. In Of Mice and Men George is the one who is loyal even though he does the killing and in The Kite Runner the main character Amir is not loyal at first and he is the one who betrays. Also Of Mice and Men is quite short and The Kite Runner is much longer. The setting is also different, one is in America and the other is in Afghanistan, so the cultures are different, and the language is different.

To conclude, both books are about loyalty and betrayal and they show it through symbols and the plot. I think that Steinbeck and Hosseini are very good writers and that these books show that betrayal can have bad effects on people and that loyalty is important in friendship. I enjoyed both of them and they are good to compare.

task: In what ways and to what effect do two works you have studied explore guilt and the possibility of atonement?
text:
Guilt is one of the oldest subjects in literature, and in Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner and Ian McEwan's Atonement it is the motor that drives the whole story. Both novels begin with a single moment of cowardice or malice in the childhood of the narrator, and then follow the long decades in which the narrator tries to put that moment right. This essay will tell the story of each novel, showing how each plot is built around guilt, and then will compare the two at the end.

The Kite Runner begins in 2001 with the narrator, Amir, now living in California, receiving a phone call from his father's old friend Rahim Khan, who tells him that there is a way to be good again. The story then goes back to Kabul in the 1970s, where Amir grows up in a wealthy house in the Wazir Akbar Khan district with his father, Baba, a successful and powerful businessman whom everybody admires. Amir's mother died giving birth to him, and he feels that Baba blames him for it. Living in a small house at the bottom of the garden are Ali, Baba's servant, and Ali's son Hassan, who is Amir's age. Ali and Hassan are Hazaras, a Shia minority looked down on by the Pashtun majority, and Amir, who is Pashtun and Sunni, sometimes treats Hassan unkindly even as they play together every day. Hassan is cheerful and loyal, and he cannot read, so Amir reads him stories and sometimes plays tricks on him by making up words to see whether he will pretend to understand.

The central event of the novel is the winter kite-fighting tournament of 1975. Amir wants to win it so that Baba will finally be proud of him. He does win, by cutting the last kite, and Hassan, who is the best kite runner in the district, runs to fetch the fallen kite for him, calling out that he will bring it back, for you a thousand times over. Amir goes looking for him and finds him in an alley, cornered by Assef, a blond, cruel boy who hates Hazaras and who has threatened Hassan before. Hassan has the blue kite, and he refuses to give it up. Assef rapes him while two other boys hold him down. Amir watches from behind a corner and does nothing; he runs away. For the rest of the winter, Amir cannot look at Hassan, and the guilt turns into resentment, because Hassan's presence reminds him of what he did. In the end Amir plants a watch and some money under Hassan's mattress and accuses him of stealing them. Hassan, to Amir's astonishment, confesses to a theft he did not commit, and Baba forgives him. Soon after, Ali and Hassan leave the house, which is what Amir had wanted and also what he comes to see as his worst crime.

In 1981, after the Soviet invasion, Amir and Baba escape to Pakistan and then to California, where they settle in Fremont. Baba works at a petrol station and sells goods at a flea market on weekends, and Amir goes to college and begins to write. Amir meets Soraya Taheri, the daughter of a former general, and they marry just before Baba dies of cancer. Amir becomes a published novelist. Years later Rahim Khan, who is ill, calls Amir to Pakistan and tells him the truth: Hassan was Baba's son, so he was Amir's half-brother, and Hassan and his wife have been killed by the Taliban, leaving a son, Sohrab, who is in an orphanage in Kabul. Amir travels to Afghanistan, which is now ruled by the Taliban, and finds that Sohrab has been taken by a Taliban official who turns out to be Assef. Assef agrees to fight Amir, and beats him badly with brass knuckles until Sohrab fires a slingshot into Assef's eye. Amir and Sohrab escape, and Amir takes the boy to America, though the adoption is complicated and Sohrab tries to kill himself after hearing he might be returned to an orphanage. The novel ends with Amir flying a kite with Sohrab in San Francisco, and Sohrab smiles for the first time. Amir runs the kite for him, saying that for you a thousand times over.

Atonement begins in a different place and a different kind of family. On a hot day in the summer of 1935, thirteen-year-old Briony Tallis, a bright and imaginative girl who loves order and writes plays, is at her family's country house in England. Her older sister Cecilia has just finished university at Cambridge, where she met Robbie Turner, the son of the family's cleaning lady, whose education has been paid for by Briony's father. There is tension between Cecilia and Robbie. By the fountain in the garden Cecilia strips to her underwear and jumps into the water to retrieve a broken piece of a vase, while Robbie watches, and Briony sees this from a window and misunderstands it. Later Robbie writes a letter to Cecilia, and by accident he puts into the envelope a version of the letter in which he uses a very crude word for what he wants. He asks Briony to deliver it, and she reads it. She thinks that Robbie is a maniac.

That night the Tallis family has a dinner party for Leon, the brother, and his friend Paul Marshall, a chocolate manufacturer, together with the twins Jackson and Pierrot, who are Briony's cousins and who have come to the house because their parents are getting a divorce. Briony finds Cecilia and Robbie in the library, where they are having sex, and she thinks that Robbie is attacking her sister. Later the twins run away, and the family go out to search for them in the dark. Briony finds her fifteen-year-old cousin Lola being raped by a man whose face she cannot see, but she tells the police that she saw Robbie do it. She says it so firmly that the family and the police believe her. Robbie is arrested and taken away, and Cecilia, who loves him, cuts herself off from her family.

The second part of the book takes place in 1940 during the retreat to Dunkirk. Robbie served three years in prison and was then released on condition that he joins the army. He is walking with two corporals through the French countryside toward the coast, thinking of Cecilia and of the letters she has written to him. He is ill from an infected wound, and in the final scenes on the beach at Dunkirk he sees the chaos of the defeated army. Part three follows Briony, now eighteen, who has become a trainee nurse in London instead of going to Cambridge, and who nurses wounded soldiers who have returned from France. She has realised that she was wrong about Robbie and wants to make amends. She visits Cecilia, who lives in a flat in Balham, and finds Robbie there. Cecilia and Robbie tell Briony that she must go to her parents, tell them the truth, and write a new statement for the police. Briony agrees to do so.

The final section is a coda, set in 1999, in which Briony is seventy-seven and a famous novelist, and is at the Tallis house, now a hotel, for her birthday. She reveals that she has been writing the novel we have just read, over her entire life, and that she has a form of dementia and will soon die. She also reveals that Robbie died of septicaemia at Dunkirk and Cecilia was killed in the bombing of Balham tube station, so that the reunion and the happy ending were fiction, invented by Briony, who could not bring herself to tell the truth of what she did. She says that because she is a novelist she has the power to decide what happens, and that she has given Robbie and Cecilia the happiness that they did not have.

Having told the two stories, it is possible to compare them briefly. In both books a child commits a wrong against an innocent person and the rest of the book is shaped by the guilt which follows. Amir and Briony are both writers, and both stories are in some sense written by the guilty person, which makes the reader wonder how far we can trust what they say. Both novels also use war as a background, the Soviet invasion and the Taliban in one and the Second World War in the other. There are differences: Amir is able to atone, in part, by saving Sohrab, while Briony's atonement is only possible in fiction because the people she wronged are dead. Overall, both novels show that guilt can last a lifetime and that atonement may be difficult or impossible, and in this they are similar even though one is set in Afghanistan and the other in England.

task: Individual oral: Examine the ways in which the global issue of forced migration is presented through the content and form of a literary extract and a non-literary text.
text:
Good morning. In this oral I want to explore how literature and non-literary writing represent the global issue of forced migration, and in particular how the language used to describe displacement can either restore a person's humanity or quietly remove it. My two texts are an extract from Mohsin Hamid's 2017 novel Exit West, from the chapter in which Nadia and Saeed step through a black door, and a press release issued by the United Nations refugee agency announcing that the number of forcibly displaced people worldwide had risen to well over a hundred million. The global issue sits in the field of culture, identity and community, and my guiding question is this: how do the form and language choices of each text shape what the reader understands displacement to be, and which kind of understanding does a world of mass migration actually need?

I will begin with the extract from Exit West, because it is the text that most obviously resists the way the issue is usually told. At this point in the novel, the city where Nadia and Saeed live is being overrun by militants and cut off from the world. They have fallen in love in the middle of the war, and they pay an agent for access to one of the mysterious doors that, in Hamid's imagined world, lead instantly to other countries. The first and most important choice Hamid makes is to introduce a fantastical device into a setting that is otherwise ruthlessly realistic. Magical realism here is not decoration. By replacing the boat, the lorry and the border fence with a door, he removes the spectacle of the journey that the news usually focuses on, and puts the weight on what happens inside the person who passes through. The door is described as dark, like a black hole, and the crossing is compared to something like dying and being born. The comparison matters because it makes migration a kind of bereavement as well as a movement. Saeed and Nadia do not simply change location; a version of themselves is left behind. Hamid writes, in a line I find very moving, that people say that when you migrate you kill off the version of you who stayed behind, and that the sorrow of this killing is something that migrants carry. The generalising voice of that sentence, with its present tense and its second person, widens a private grief into a universal condition.

The sentence structure supports this. Hamid is known for long, flowing sentences held together by commas and the word and, and in this extract the syntax moves like the people it describes: unbroken, a little breathless, without a place to stop. When the sentences finally shorten at the moment of crossing, the effect is almost physical, like a held breath released. The narration is third person and omniscient, but it slips between Nadia's and Saeed's perspectives, and that is important for my argument, because it refuses to treat the couple as a single anonymous unit. Each of them has a different fear. Saeed is thinking about his father, whom he is leaving behind, and Nadia is thinking about the freedom she is going toward and the independence she has fought to keep. So Hamid individualises the refugee, giving her interior life and contradictory feelings. He also uses a quiet irony: the agent who sells the passage is shown as a small, tired, practical man, not a villain, which complicates the stereotype of the exploitative smuggler and suggests that the economics of migration are made by the same desperation that creates the migrants.

Now I turn to the second text, the press release from the UN refugee agency. Its purpose is entirely different. It is an informative and persuasive text, designed to be quoted by journalists and to put pressure on governments and donors. Its register is formal and institutional, and the first thing that stands out is the headline statistic, placed at the beginning in the position of greatest emphasis. A round number above a hundred million tells the reader that the scale is historic, and the verbs used for the change, such as risen or reached, treat displacement as a natural force with a graph, a force that is happening rather than being done by anybody. The syntax is full of passive constructions and nominalisations: people are displaced, populations are affected, needs are growing. Agents disappear. The reader is told that conflict, persecution and climate-related disasters are causes, but not who is responsible for the conflicts, which is understandable in a text that must stay politically neutral in order to keep access to the countries it works in. The terminology is also revealing. The people in the report are persons of concern, internally displaced persons and asylum seekers, categories that exist in international law and that determine what help a person can receive. This is a language of classification, and it is necessary. But it means that Nadia, who in Hamid's novel is a woman who rides a motorcycle and is wary of the religion she was raised in, would appear in this text as a unit in a column.

However, I would not want to argue that the press release dehumanises. It does something Hamid cannot do, which is to hold a whole planet in one sentence. Its statistics are a way of making a claim on the world's attention, and the document does move at several points from the number to a single person, usually in a short quotation or a named case, because its writers know that figures alone do not move readers. The structure, then, is a deliberate alternation between abstraction and example, and this is a rhetorical strategy: the statistics create urgency and the individual story creates sympathy. I find it significant that the text needs the literary technique of the case study to do its job, while the novel, for its part, needs a large-scale frame to avoid being a private love story. Hamid supplies this in other parts of the book, where doors begin to open across the world, in London, in Tokyo, in San Francisco, and the whole planet is transformed into a place of constant arrival. The extract I have chosen belongs to the small-scale half of that design, and the press release belongs to the large-scale half.

Putting the two texts together reveals three things about the issue. First, both texts treat displacement as normal rather than exceptional. The press release does so by showing a steady upward trend, and Hamid does so through the book's refrain that we are all migrants through time, which turns the sentence of the refugee into a condition of being alive. Second, the two texts differ in who they let speak. The press release speaks about migrants, with an institutional voice that is confident and unified. The novel speaks from within and between them, with a narrator who is uncertain, who uses the phrase it is said, and who admits that some things cannot be known. Third, and this is the point I find most challenging, the texts imply different ideas of what a reader ought to do. The press release wants an action, a donation or a policy, and the novel wants a recognition, the sense that the people in the dark door are like us. My view is that neither is adequate alone. A reader moved only by Nadia and Saeed can mistake pity for solidarity, and a reader convinced only by the statistics can treat a hundred million as a problem of logistics. The global issue of forced migration is therefore partly an issue of language: we need both the classification that makes help possible and the narrative that makes the person visible.

Finally, I want to acknowledge a limitation in my own approach. I have treated the press release as a representative of institutional writing, but it is only one text and a particular one, produced by an organisation with an interest in the problem being seen as large. Hamid, too, is a writer writing from relative comfort about a journey he did not take as a refugee, and his choice of a magical door could be criticised as making the dangers of real crossings too painless. I think that the door is better understood as a way of testing what migration means when the journey is removed, and the novel does not pretend that arrival is safe, since Nadia and Saeed meet hostility and violence in London. Even so, the question of who has the right to represent displacement remains open, and I think it is the most important one this global issue raises. To conclude, forced migration is presented by these two texts as both a mass phenomenon and an intimate loss, and it is only when the reader holds both of those views at once that the issue can be properly understood. Thank you.

task: Individual oral: Examine the ways in which the global issue of the role of gender and power in society is presented through a literary extract and a non-literary text.
text:
Hello. The global issue I have chosen for my oral is gender and power in society, which comes under the field of politics, power and justice. My two texts are an extract from The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood, which is a novel published in 1985, and a magazine advertisement from the 1950s for a vacuum cleaner which shows a woman happily using it while her husband sits reading the newspaper. I chose them because they both show how women have been controlled in different ways and I think this is still a big issue today. First I am going to talk about the extract, then the advertisement, then I will compare them and give my conclusion.

The extract from The Handmaid's Tale is from the chapter where Offred takes part in the Ceremony, in which the Commander tries to have a child with her while Serena Joy, his wife, holds her hands. The book is set in Gilead, which used to be the United States but has been taken over by a religious regime where women are not allowed to work, own money or read. Offred is a Handmaid, which means that her only role is to give birth to a child for the Commander and his wife because most of the women are infertile due to pollution. In the extract Atwood describes the Ceremony in a very cold way. Offred lies on her back with her head on Serena Joy's stomach and the Commander is at the other end, and she says that this is not exactly rape because she signed up for it, though there was not much choice. She also says that nothing is going on here that I haven't signed up for.

Atwood uses a lot of techniques in this extract. The first one is first person narration, because the book is told by Offred. This makes the reader feel close to her and it makes us understand how she feels. It is also in the present tense in the extract, which makes it feel as though it is happening at that moment and this makes it more shocking. There are many short sentences which make it sound emotionless, because Offred has learned to detach herself and stop her mind from being there. Atwood also uses a lot of imagery. For example she describes the room, where there is a canopy and a white bed and the carpets, and the bed is compared to something that is trying to suffocate. She also uses the symbol of the colour red, because the Handmaids wear red, which can stand for blood and fertility but also danger. The word Ceremony is also a euphemism, because it makes a rape sound like a religious ritual, and this shows how Gilead uses language to hide what it does. I think that Atwood did this so that we will think about what could happen if women's rights were taken away.

The second text is the vacuum cleaner advertisement. It is from a magazine in the 1950s and it has a picture of a woman in a dress with her hair neat and she is smiling at the vacuum cleaner. In the background the husband is in a chair. The main slogan is in large letters and says something like give her the gift she really wants, and below it are paragraphs of smaller text which list the features of the machine. The target audience is probably men, because it is telling them what to buy for their wives, but it could also be women who are shown what they should want. The purpose of the advertisement is to persuade people to buy the product, and it does it by using emotive language and by showing that the housewife will be happier if she has the machine.

The advertisement uses several techniques as well. It uses a direct address with the word you, which makes the reader feel that the advert is talking to them. It uses a bright colour scheme with pink and yellow, which are traditionally seen as feminine colours, and this stereotypes women. The picture is posed, because the woman is smiling in an unrealistic way, which shows that housework is presented as pleasure and not as work. The text is full of positive adjectives like beautiful, effortless and new. There is also a rule of three in the slogan, which makes it memorable. The advertisement assumes that a woman's place is in the home and that cleaning is her job and not a job for her husband, who is only shown reading, so this shows that men had power and women did not.

Now I am going to compare them. Both texts show women in a domestic role which is decided by men. In The Handmaid's Tale the role is enforced by law and violence, and in the advertisement it is enforced by culture and by the expectations of the time, but both of them are about control. Both texts also use language to hide the reality: Atwood's Gilead calls rape a Ceremony, and the advert calls housework a gift. One difference is the genre, because the novel is fiction and the advert is non-fiction and made to sell something. Another difference is that the novel is critical of the system and the advertisement supports it, so the first is trying to warn the reader and the second is trying to sell. Another difference is the tone, which is dark and sad in the novel and cheerful in the advertisement.

I also think the texts are connected to the global issue because gender inequality is still an issue in many countries. In some countries women do not have the same rights as men, for example in Afghanistan, where the Taliban have banned girls from secondary school, and in many countries women still do more of the housework than men and are paid less. The Handmaid's Tale has become popular again in recent years, and women have worn the red cloaks and white bonnets in protests, for example about abortion laws in the United States, which shows that the book is still relevant. Atwood herself has said that she did not put anything in the novel that had not already happened somewhere in history, which makes it more disturbing. The advertisement shows how gender roles were presented in the past, and although it looks old fashioned, there are still adverts today which show women doing the cleaning and men doing the cooking only as a joke.

In conclusion, both texts show how women can be controlled by power, in one case by the state and in the other by society. The Handmaid's Tale shows an extreme example and the advertisement shows an ordinary one, and the two of them together show a range. They help us understand the global issue of gender and power because they show that inequality can be dramatic or it can be quiet and normal, and that language is used in both cases to make it look acceptable. I think that the global issue is important and that people need to keep reading books like this and challenging adverts like that so that gender inequality will continue to be talked about. Thank you for listening.

task: Individual oral: Examine the ways in which the global issue of the human impact on the environment is presented through a literary extract and a non-literary text.
text:
Okay so my global issue is climate change and the environment, which is in the field of science, technology and the environment. My two texts are a poem by Gerard Manley Hopkins called Binsey Poplars and a speech by Greta Thunberg at the United Nations, the one where she says how dare you. I think these two texts are about how humans are destroying nature and this is a problem all over the world.

I'll start with the poem. Binsey Poplars is about some poplar trees that were cut down near Oxford in the nineteenth century. Hopkins was a priest as well as a poet and he loved nature, so he was sad when the trees were cut down. In the first lines he says my aspens dear and then he says they have all been felled, felled, are all felled. So he repeats the word felled a lot of times, and this shows that he is very upset and it also sounds like the sound of an axe hitting the tree. He also uses a lot of alliteration and imagery, and the leaves are compared to something, I think it is cages, and the sun is leaping in the leaves. The poem is about nature and how nature is beautiful and humans destroy it for no reason. He says that after-comers cannot guess the beauty been, which means that the people in the future will never know how beautiful the trees were. I think this relates to climate change because we are also destroying nature now and the people in the future will suffer.

The poem has a rhyme scheme and it has some long lines and short lines. The stanzas are not all the same. The mood is sad and angry. The tone is also kind of religious because Hopkins was a priest so he thinks that nature is made by God and humans should not destroy it. I think that the poem is the literary text because it is a poem and it uses poetic devices like metaphor and personification, because the trees are called dear and they are almost like people.

Now the second text, which is the speech by Greta Thunberg. Greta Thunberg is a young Swedish climate activist who started a school strike for climate and became famous. She gave the speech at the UN climate action summit in New York in 2019. In the speech she is very angry and she says that the leaders have stolen her dreams and her childhood with their empty words. She says how dare you many times and this is repetition and it is also a rhetorical question. This makes the audience feel guilty and it makes them listen. She also uses statistics, for example she talks about the carbon budget and how little time we have left, and she also talks about money and about eternal economic growth, which she calls a fairy tale. She uses the pronoun you to blame the leaders and she says that the young people are watching. The speech is a non-literary text because it is a speech and it is meant to persuade people, and its purpose is to make leaders take action on climate change.

The two texts are similar because they are both about humans damaging nature and they are both emotional. Both of them are angry and sad, and both of them use repetition, felled felled and how dare you. They are also different because the poem is from the 1800s and the speech is from 2019 and one is a poem and one is a speech. Hopkins is writing about a small thing which is a few trees and Greta is talking about the whole planet. Also the poem is more quiet and the speech is loud.

In conclusion, the texts show the global issue of human impact on the environment and they show that humans destroy nature. Both writers want people to change what they are doing. I think that the issue is very important because if we do not do something then there will be a lot of floods and fires and the planet will get too hot, and the poem and the speech both help us to understand this. That is the end of my oral, thank you.

task: Economics: Evaluate the effectiveness of indirect taxes as a policy to correct the negative externalities of consumption.
text:
A negative externality of consumption arises when the consumption of a good imposes costs on third parties who are not part of the transaction, so that the marginal social cost (MSC) of consumption is lower than the marginal social benefit would justify at the market outcome. In the case of sugary drinks, for example, consumers account for their own pleasure and price, but not for the cost to the health service of treating obesity and type 2 diabetes. In an unregulated market, consumers choose where marginal private benefit (MPB) equals price, which is above the socially optimal quantity, so the market overconsumes the good and there is a welfare loss. An indirect tax is a tax on expenditure, imposed on the producer or seller, and it is the standard market-based remedy. This essay will argue that indirect taxes are an effective but imperfect tool: they work best where demand is not too inelastic and the external cost can be estimated, and they are often most effective as part of a package of policies.

The theory is straightforward. In a diagram with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, the market equilibrium is where supply, which reflects marginal private cost, meets demand, which is MPB, at Qm. Where consumption causes a negative externality, the MSB curve lies below the MPB curve, and the optimal output is at Qopt, where MSB meets supply. A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost shifts the supply curve upwards by the amount of the tax. The price paid by consumers rises, the quantity falls from Qm to Qopt, and the welfare loss triangle, which measures the net social cost of overconsumption between Qopt and Qm, is eliminated. Government also collects tax revenue, equal to the tax per unit multiplied by Qopt, which can be used to fund the health service or to cut other taxes, an advantage that regulation does not offer. This is the Pigouvian principle of internalising the externality: the price now reflects the full cost of consumption.

Evidence from real markets suggests that the approach can work. The UK introduced its Soft Drinks Industry Levy in 2018, with two tiers based on the amount of sugar per 100 millilitres. A distinctive design feature is that the levy is paid by producers and importers rather than being a flat tax on all soft drinks, so it created a strong incentive to reformulate. Many manufacturers reduced the sugar in their drinks to fall below the thresholds, and the average sugar content of drinks subject to the levy fell by a substantial share, with much of the change coming from supply-side reformulation rather than from consumers cutting their consumption. In Mexico, a tax of one peso per litre on sugar-sweetened drinks was introduced in 2014, and studies found that purchases of taxed drinks fell by roughly six per cent in the first year, with the fall larger among lower-income households. Both cases show that an indirect tax can change behaviour and generate revenue, so the policy is effective in directing resources away from the over-produced good.

However, effectiveness depends on elasticity. If the price elasticity of demand (PED) for the good is inelastic, a given tax will cause only a small reduction in quantity, and most of the tax will be passed on to consumers as higher prices, which means that the burden falls on them rather than on the producer. For addictive goods such as cigarettes, PED is low, perhaps between minus 0.3 and minus 0.5 in high-income countries, so a 10 per cent rise in price might reduce consumption by only 3 to 5 per cent. In this case the tax achieves less correction than the diagram suggests, although it raises considerable revenue. Taxes on sugary drinks are more effective, because close substitutes such as water and diet drinks are readily available, which makes demand more elastic. Evaluation of any tax therefore requires a judgment about elasticity, and this is itself uncertain, since PED varies over time, and between groups of consumers. In the short run, consumers may keep buying while they adjust, but over several years the response is usually larger.

A second limitation is the difficulty of measuring the external cost. For the tax to equal the marginal external cost, the government would need to know the monetary value of the harm, including the costs of treating illness, lost productivity, and also the harm to the individuals who consume it, called internalities, which are often difficult to calculate. In practice governments choose a tax rate through political judgment and then adjust it. If the tax is set too low, there will still be overconsumption; if it is too high, there will be underconsumption and a welfare loss on the other side of the optimum. Government failure is therefore a real risk, since the rate may reflect the lobbying power of industry and the need for revenue as much as an estimate of external costs. There is also the problem that when a tax raises revenue, governments have a financial interest in consumption continuing, which may weaken the incentive to reduce it.

A third concern is equity. Indirect taxes are regressive, taking a larger proportion of income from poorer households, who tend to spend a larger share of their income on goods such as tobacco and sugary drinks. In the Mexican example the largest reduction in purchases was among lower-income households, which suggests that these households also gained most in health terms, but if demand is inelastic, they will pay more for the same quantity and be worse off. The policy can be made fairer if the revenue is earmarked for example for subsidised school meals or healthcare, but this depends on government decisions and not on the tax itself. Evaluation of the policy depends on the weight given to equity compared with efficiency, which is a normative judgment.

Other policies may be more suitable in some cases. Regulation, such as banning a good, is simple and effective where the harm is severe, but it removes consumer choice and may create an illegal market. Education and nudges, such as warning labels, may help when consumers underestimate the harm, but the evidence is that on their own they are slow and modest in effect. Subsidising alternatives such as healthy food can offset the regressive effect of a tax. For a global externality like carbon emissions, a national indirect tax might lead to carbon leakage if firms move production to countries with lower taxes, so tradable permits or international agreement may be better. The evidence suggests that no single instrument is sufficient in every case.

In conclusion, indirect taxes can be an effective way of correcting the negative externalities of consumption, particularly where there are close substitutes and the external cost is well understood, as the experience in the UK and Mexico illustrates. Their effectiveness is limited by inelastic demand, imprecise estimates of the external cost, regressivity and the risk of government failure. On balance I judge them to be a valuable component rather than a complete solution: they are most convincing when the revenue is used progressively and the tax is combined with information and, where necessary, regulation.

task: Business Management: Evaluate the view that financial rewards are the most effective way of motivating employees.
text:
Motivation is the desire and willingness of a person to put effort into their work. It is very important for a business because motivated workers are more productive, absent less often, and are less likely to leave, which means that the business saves money on recruitment and training. There are many ways that a business can try to motivate its employees and these can be divided into financial and non-financial methods. In this essay I will explain financial methods of motivation and non-financial methods and then decide whether financial rewards are the most effective way.

Financial methods of motivation are those which use money to encourage employees to work harder. The first is salary, which is a fixed amount of pay each year and is usually paid monthly. The second is wages, which are paid by the hour or by the week, and sometimes with overtime. The third is piece rate, where employees are paid for each unit that they produce, which is common in factories and in agriculture. The fourth is commission, where salespeople are paid a percentage of the value of their sales. Other financial methods are bonuses, profit sharing, performance related pay, and fringe benefits such as a company car or health insurance.

The theory which supports the use of financial rewards is F. W. Taylor's scientific management. Taylor believed that workers were motivated mainly by money and that they would work harder if they were paid more, so he recommended piece rate and detailed supervision. This theory is sometimes called an economic man view of workers. Taylor was writing in the early twentieth century and he worked in steel factories, where the work was repetitive. According to Taylor, managers should break jobs down into small tasks and pay people for how much they produce, and this would increase output. An advantage of financial methods is that they are easy to understand and they can be linked directly to performance, so that the employee can see the reward for working harder. They are also useful in jobs where the output can be measured, such as sales.

However, there are also disadvantages. Financial rewards are expensive for the business and they can increase the costs, so profit might fall. They might also cause employees to focus on quantity rather than quality, because piece rate pushes workers to produce as many units as possible and quality may go down, and commission may cause salespeople to use pressure selling and upset customers. If the rewards are removed or reduced the employees may be demotivated. Also, a financial reward only works for a short time, because after some time people get used to the money and want more.

Non-financial methods of motivation do not use money. These include job enrichment, job rotation, job enlargement, empowerment, teamwork, recognition, and training. Job enrichment means giving employees more challenging and interesting tasks, and job rotation means moving workers between jobs to reduce boredom. Empowerment means giving employees the power to make decisions. Recognition might be a thank you or an employee of the month award. Training can help employees to develop and to get promoted.

The theories behind these are Maslow and Herzberg. Maslow's hierarchy of needs has five levels, which are physiological needs, safety needs, social needs, esteem needs and self-actualisation. Maslow said that when a lower need is met, the person is motivated by the next one up. A business should therefore find out which level its workers are on. Money helps to satisfy the lower needs, such as food and shelter and security, but it does not satisfy the higher needs, such as esteem and self-actualisation, so a business should use non-financial methods as well. Herzberg's two factor theory says that there are hygiene factors and motivators. Hygiene factors are things like pay, working conditions, job security and company policy, and if they are poor the employees will be dissatisfied, but making them better does not motivate people. Motivators are things like achievement, recognition, responsibility and the work itself, and these lead to satisfaction and to motivation. So according to Herzberg, pay is not a motivator, and a business which uses only financial rewards will not motivate its workers for long.

The advantages of non-financial methods are that they are often cheaper than financial rewards and they can create a longer lasting effect, because the workers feel that they are valued, and they may be more loyal to the business. Some companies, such as Google, are famous for having a good working environment with free food, games and flexible working, and as a result they attract talented staff and have low staff turnover. However, there are also disadvantages. Training and job enrichment can cost money and time, and not every employee wants more responsibility, since some employees prefer simple jobs. Some of the methods take a long time to have an effect, and if the pay is too low, then no amount of non-financial methods will motivate the staff, as a worker has to be able to pay the rent.

In my opinion, financial rewards are important but they are not always the most effective way to motivate employees. It depends on the type of business, on the kind of employees and on the situation. For example, in a call centre or in a factory where the work is repetitive, financial rewards might work better because the workers are doing the same task over and over, and there is not much opportunity for job enrichment. In contrast, in a creative company or in a hospital, where the workers care about the work, non-financial methods may be more effective. It also depends on the culture, because in some countries the people value job security more than pay. Another factor is the size of the business, because a small business may not have the money to pay large bonuses, so it may rely more on teamwork and recognition.

In conclusion, I believe that financial rewards are not the most effective way of motivating employees on their own, because of the evidence from Herzberg and Maslow that people also need to feel valued and to have interesting work. The best approach for a business is to use a combination of both financial and non-financial methods, so that the employees are paid fairly and also have job satisfaction. If a business does this, it will have a more motivated workforce, higher productivity and higher profits in the long run.

task: Geography: Examine the causes and consequences of rural to urban migration in low-income countries.
text:
Rural to urban migration is when people move from the countryside to the city. This happens a lot in low income countries like India, Brazil and Nigeria. There are many causes and consequences of this and in this essay I will explain them.

The causes of rural to urban migration can be put into push factors and pull factors. Push factors are the things that push people out of the countryside. One of these is that there is not enough jobs in the countryside and people are poor. Farming is hard and people do not get paid much money. Another push factor is drought and floods which destroy the crops, so the farmers have no food and they have to leave. There are also not many schools and hospitals in rural areas. In some places there is war or conflict. Pull factors are things that pull people to the city. Cities have more jobs in factories and offices, and the wages are higher. There are better schools and hospitals and there is electricity and running water. People think that life is better in the city and that they will get rich, because they see it on the television or because their family members who moved there tell them.

There are also consequences of rural to urban migration. For the cities, there is a lot of population growth and the city becomes overcrowded. This leads to the growth of slums, which are also called shanty towns or informal settlements, where people live in houses made from wood and metal and there is no clean water or toilets. In Mumbai in India there is a large slum called Dharavi where a lot of people live and diseases spread easily. There is also a lot of traffic and pollution in cities and crime and unemployment because there are not enough jobs for everyone. The government has to spend money on housing and services and it cannot afford it.

There are also positive consequences for cities, because the migrants provide cheap labour, and the economy grows. Some of the migrants send money back to their families in the countryside, which is called remittances, and this helps the rural area. But it is also bad for the rural areas because mainly young people leave and then there are mostly old people and children left, so there is no one to work on the farm. The villages can become empty and the schools shut down.

To solve the problems, governments can do things like build more houses and create jobs in the countryside so that people don't need to leave. They can improve the services in rural areas, such as schools, hospitals and roads. Also, they can improve the slums by giving them electricity and water. Some governments have tried to make new cities.

In conclusion, there are many causes of rural to urban migration, push and pull factors, and it has both good and bad consequences. I think that it has more bad consequences than good because of the slums. The governments need to do something about it so that the cities will not become too crowded.

task: Historical investigation: To what extent was the Marshall Plan responsible for the economic recovery of Western Europe between 1947 and 1951? (Sections: identification and evaluation of sources, investigation, reflection.)
text:
Section 1: Identification and evaluation of sources

The investigation asks to what extent the Marshall Plan was responsible for Western Europe's economic recovery between 1947 and 1951. Two sources are evaluated: George C. Marshall's address at the Harvard commencement on 5 June 1947, as printed in the Department of State Bulletin on 15 June 1947 (Source A), and the concluding chapters of Alan S. Milward's The Reconstruction of Western Europe, 1945-51, published in 1984 (Source B).

Source A is the speech in which the American Secretary of State first publicly proposed a programme of aid for Europe. Its origin is significant. Marshall was speaking as the senior American diplomat, to a graduating audience, but the real audience was European governments and the American Congress, and the choice of a university platform rather than a diplomatic occasion was deliberate. Its purpose was to invite Europeans to take the initiative: Marshall said that the programme should be a joint one, agreed by some, if not all, European nations, and that the United States would assist in drafting only on the basis of European proposals. He also said the policy was directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos. The content is valuable because it shows how the American government wished the plan to be seen, as humanitarian and constructive, and as a response to the dollar shortage that was threatening to halt European purchases of American goods. It also shows that the plan was originally conceived as a way to remove obstacles to recovery rather than as the origin of recovery. Its limitations are equally clear. It was a statement of intent, with no figures, no timetable and no aid yet delivered, so it cannot tell us what the plan actually achieved. Its careful language also hides motives that other evidence reveals, since the speech avoids mentioning the fear of Communist electoral success in France and Italy, and the offer was framed so that Stalin could, in theory, decline without Marshall having excluded him.

Source B was written by a British economic historian who had worked on the official history of war production and who drew on archives of several European governments, including their finance ministries. Written nearly forty years after the events, it has the benefit of hindsight and of declassified records. Milward's purpose is explicitly revisionist: he is arguing against the older, largely American view that the plan saved Europe from collapse, and he contends that national recovery strategies, rather than American aid, shaped the post-war economic order, with the aid being a small proportion of national investment. The value of the source is its detailed use of national economic records and its willingness to test the claim about American generosity against the figures. Its limitations arise from the same thesis. Because Milward writes against an orthodoxy, he may understate what the aid did in 1947-48, when scarce dollars were decisive for the imports of fuel and food, and his emphasis on national governments gives less weight to the political and psychological effect of the plan. The two sources therefore pose opposite pictures, a statement of American intention and a later scholarly challenge to its importance, and the investigation will test one against the other.

Section 2: Investigation

The Marshall Plan, officially the European Recovery Program, delivered roughly 13 billion dollars of American aid to sixteen European countries between 1948 and 1951, with Britain receiving the largest share, about 3.2 billion, followed by France, with 2.7 billion, and with Italy and West Germany each receiving about 1.4 to 1.5 billion. In absolute terms this was a vast sum, but as a share of the recipients' combined national income it was around two to three per cent per year, which is the starting point for Milward's argument that it cannot have been the main driver of recovery. This investigation argues that the plan was a necessary but not sufficient cause, which was decisive in one specific respect, the removal of the dollar constraint in 1947-49, but that the recovery itself rested mostly on domestic policy, on structural factors and on international trade arrangements.

The case that recovery was already under way is persuasive. By 1947 industrial production in much of Western Europe was already approaching, and in some countries exceeding, pre-war levels, helped by the pent-up demand of the war years and by the high investment made possible by wartime destruction of obsolete capacity. In France the Monnet Plan, adopted in 1946, directed investment toward coal, steel, electricity and transport, and French output had risen substantially before the first Marshall dollar arrived. In Britain, the Labour government's austerity, export drives and nationalisation programme were attempting to rebuild the balance of payments. These facts back Milward's view that governments, committed to full employment and to the welfare state, were the principal agents of recovery, and they undermine the claim in the speech that Europe faced economic collapse without American aid.

However, the crisis of 1947 was real, and it was a crisis of one particular kind. The severe winter of 1946-47 disrupted coal production and transport, and as European industry recovered, it needed imports of American food, machinery, cotton and fuel that it could not pay for, because it did not earn enough dollars from exports. This dollar gap meant that further recovery would have required either import cuts, or deflationary policies, or a collapse of trade with the dollar area. Marshall aid financed the gap. It enabled governments to continue investing and importing without squeezing living standards still further, which in countries such as France and Italy, where Communist parties had considerable electoral support, carried a political risk as well as an economic one. In this respect, Source A's description of the purpose of the plan is vindicated, and Milward's claim is weakened: the aid did not create recovery, but it kept it from stalling. The counterpart funds mechanism reinforced this effect. Governments sold American goods to local buyers, deposited the proceeds in local-currency funds, and used them with American approval for reconstruction and for reducing budget deficits, which supported monetary stability.

The most important independent factor is the German currency reform of June 1948, which replaced the Reichsmark with the Deutschmark and, under Ludwig Erhard, ended most price controls. The reform restored incentives to produce and sell goods that had been hoarded under the old system, and industrial output in the Western zones rose quickly in the following months. It is tempting to attribute this to Marshall aid, but the reform was an administrative and monetary measure which owed little to American money, and Germany received less aid than Britain or France. Here Milward's scepticism seems justified. At the same time, one should recognise that the reform was designed with American direction in the occupied zones, so that the line between American influence and domestic initiative is blurred.

A second structural contribution of the plan was institutional. The United States required European recipients to cooperate through the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation, created in 1948, and the OEEC's work led in 1950 to the European Payments Union, which allowed members to settle trade balances multilaterally without needing dollars. Intra-European trade increased rapidly as a result, and it was an important engine of growth in the early 1950s. Historians such as Michael Hogan have stressed this dimension, arguing that the plan was an attempt to export American ideas about productivity and integration, which makes the plan's long-term influence larger than its immediate financial contribution. This view is not available in Source A, which says little about integration, and Milward treats it with scepticism, believing that the changes were pursued mostly out of national interest.

Finally, other explanations compete. The Korean War boom of 1950-51 increased demand for European exports and fuelled rearmament spending, which changed the economic climate more than the withdrawal of Marshall aid did. The currency devaluations of 1949, including that of sterling, improved competitiveness. These factors suggest that by 1951 the recovery was self-sustaining and that the plan was winding down because it was no longer needed.

Taken together, the evidence supports a middle position. The Marshall Plan was not the main cause of recovery, as the American narrative implied, and Milward is right that national strategies and structural factors mattered more. But Milward's view understates the decisive role of the aid in 1947-49, when the dollar shortage was the binding constraint, and in building the institutions that integrated Western European trade. The plan is best seen as a catalyst which allowed a recovery that was already under way to continue at a high pace without political crisis.

Section 3: Reflection

The investigation showed me how much a historian's conclusions depend on the kind of source consulted. When I began, I expected Marshall's speech to be the basis of the story, and I assumed that the plan's importance would be evident from American statements. Reading Milward made me realise that a speech states intentions rather than outcomes, and that a statement of purpose cannot answer a question about causation. The method that proved most useful was to compare the claims of sources written at different times for different purposes, and to look for the points where one could be tested against the other, such as the share of national income represented by the aid.

The investigation also showed me the challenges of the historian's craft. The central difficulty was counterfactual: a claim that the plan was responsible for recovery implies a judgement about what would have happened without it, and this cannot be observed. I dealt with this by separating the periods and mechanisms, since the aid's effect on the dollar gap in 1947-49 is more testable than its effect on growth in general, but I recognise that this makes my conclusion a judgement of probability rather than proof. A further challenge was the historiography itself. Milward's revisionism and Hogan's emphasis on integration are products of different decades and arguments, and I came to see that a historian's interpretation is shaped by contemporary concerns as well as by evidence.

There were limitations to my approach. I worked from published speeches, translated statistics and secondary works, and I could not consult the archives of the Economic Cooperation Administration or of national finance ministries, which would have allowed me to check Milward's figures. My focus on Western Europe also meant that I paid little attention to the Soviet response, which could have shown how the political purposes of the plan were perceived. If I did the investigation again, I would add a contemporary European source, for example from a French or Italian minister, to see how the aid was understood by the recipients. Overall, the exercise taught me to treat any single explanation of a complex event with caution, and to judge the extent of a cause by asking what it was necessary for, not only whether it mattered.

task: Historical investigation: Why did Britain follow a policy of appeasement towards Germany in 1938? (Sections: identification and evaluation of sources, investigation, reflection.)
text:
Section 1: Identification and evaluation of sources

The investigation question is why Britain followed a policy of appeasement towards Germany in 1938. Two sources have been chosen. Source A is the radio broadcast made by the British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain on 27 September 1938. Source B is an extract from The Origins of the Second World War by the historian A. J. P. Taylor, published in 1961.

Source A is a speech by Chamberlain to the British people during the Sudeten crisis, when it looked as if there would be a war over Czechoslovakia. In the broadcast Chamberlain says that it is horrible, fantastic and incredible that people are digging trenches and trying on gas masks because of a quarrel in a faraway country between people of whom we know nothing. He also says that he would not hesitate to pay a third visit to Germany if he thought it would do any good. The origin of the source is that it was made by the Prime Minister himself, who was the person who decided policy, so it is useful because it shows what he thought at the time and what he wanted the public to believe. The purpose of the broadcast was to prepare people for the possibility of war but also to explain why he was still trying to find a peaceful solution, so he wanted to keep public support. The value of the source is that it is a primary source and it shows the attitude of the British government. However, the source has limitations, because Chamberlain was a politician and he may not be telling the truth about what he really thought, and because it is only a short speech so it does not give all the reasons for appeasement. It also does not mention the military situation, which was an important reason.

Source B is by A. J. P. Taylor, a famous British historian who taught at Oxford. Taylor argues that Hitler was not carrying out a master plan but was an opportunist like other German statesmen, and that the Western powers were not foolish in what they did because they were reacting to events. Taylor says that Munich was a triumph for British policy, which was to settle grievances and to avoid war. The origin of the source is that it was written by a professional historian more than twenty years after the events, so he had access to documents and hindsight. The purpose of the book was to present a new interpretation, and it was controversial and many historians disagreed with it. The value of the source is that it is a well researched secondary source that gives an overview of the reasons for appeasement. The limitation is that Taylor was known for deliberately provoking people and for putting forward unusual views, and he wrote before many British documents had been released, so he did not see everything. Also he was writing in the Cold War, which might have influenced him.

Section 2: Investigation

Appeasement was the policy followed by British governments in the 1930s of giving way to the demands of Germany in order to avoid war. In 1938 the policy reached its peak with the Anschluss in March and the Munich Agreement in September. There are many reasons why Britain followed this policy and this investigation will look at military weakness, public opinion, economic problems, the memory of the First World War, and the personality of Chamberlain.

The first reason was military weakness. By 1938 the British armed forces were not ready for a war. During the 1920s the government had followed the Ten Year Rule, which assumed that there would be no major war for ten years, and then the Depression made rearmament very expensive. Rearmament did start in 1936 and the government began to build new aeroplanes such as the Spitfire and the Hurricane, and radar stations were built along the coast, but the Royal Air Force was still not strong enough. The Chiefs of Staff told the government in 1938 that Britain was not able to fight Germany, Italy and Japan all at the same time, and that it would be dangerous to fight over Czechoslovakia. So the government decided that it was better to buy time and to continue rearming. This explains why Chamberlain went to Germany to meet Hitler at Berchtesgaden, Godesberg and finally Munich.

The second reason was public opinion. Many British people remembered the horrors of the First World War, in which nearly a million men from Britain and the Empire had died, and they were strongly in favour of peace. In 1933 the Oxford Union debated that the house would not fight for king and country, and in 1935 the Peace Ballot found that most of the people who voted supported the League of Nations and disarmament. The government was afraid of bombing, since newspapers and films like Things to Come had shown that cities could be destroyed from the air. After the Munich Agreement Chamberlain was greeted with cheering crowds, and the broadcast in Source A shows that he was aware of this feeling when he spoke about the trenches and the gas masks.

The third reason was economic. Britain had suffered in the Great Depression and the government was worried that heavy spending on rearmament would cause inflation and harm the economy. The Treasury, led by Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain until 1937, was determined to keep the budget balanced, and Britain also had a large empire to protect with limited resources. The Dominions, such as Canada and South Africa, did not want to go to war over Czechoslovakia, which made the government nervous that the Empire would not stay united. Another factor was that many British people believed that the Treaty of Versailles had been too harsh on Germany, so that the demands of Hitler to unite with Austria and to include Sudeten Germans were reasonable. They thought that self-determination was a principle which should be respected.

The fourth reason was fear of Communism. Some people in the Conservative Party, for example, were more afraid of the Soviet Union than of Germany, and they thought that a strong Germany could be a barrier to Communism in Europe. The Soviet Union was not invited to Munich. Chamberlain himself did not trust Stalin, and he believed that the Soviet army had been weakened by the purges.

The last reason is the personality of Chamberlain. Chamberlain had strong confidence in his own ability and he took control of foreign policy from the Foreign Office, and in February 1938 Anthony Eden resigned as Foreign Secretary because he disagreed with his approach to Italy. Chamberlain was a businessman and he believed that problems could be solved by sensible people talking to each other and by making reasonable compromises. He believed that Hitler could be trusted when he said that the Sudetenland was his last territorial demand. After signing the Munich Agreement he waved a piece of paper and said that it meant peace for our time, but only six months later in March 1939 Hitler occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia, and the policy of appeasement ended.

All of these reasons were important. Taylor in Source B says that the policy was sensible given the circumstances, and I agree with some of his argument because the military weakness and the public opinion were strong reasons. But other historians have said that appeasement was a mistake because Czechoslovakia had a strong army and good defences in the Sudeten mountains, and Britain gave away an ally. In conclusion, Britain followed appeasement in 1938 because of military weakness, public opinion, economic problems, fear of Communism and the character of Chamberlain, and the main reason was probably the military weakness because the government did not think it could win a war.

Section 3: Reflection

This investigation has shown me some of the problems that historians face. One of the main problems was finding sources that could be trusted. Chamberlain's broadcast is a primary source but it was a speech by a politician so it may be biased, and Taylor's book is a secondary source so it is also only one opinion. I learned that you must use different sources and compare them in order to get a more balanced view. Another problem was that there are so many reasons for appeasement that it was difficult to decide which was the most important, and different historians have different opinions about this.

I also learned that it is difficult for historians to be objective, because they are affected by the time they live in. For example, Taylor wrote in the 1960s when people already knew that appeasement had failed, and some earlier writers like the so-called Guilty Men had blamed Chamberlain for everything. So the way a historian sees the past can change over time. If I did this investigation again I would use more primary sources, such as diaries or Cabinet minutes, and I would look at the views of other countries, for example France and Czechoslovakia, because I only looked at Britain. I also would have liked to read more historians, because I only used a few books and websites. Overall I found that history is not just about facts but also about interpretation, and this was an interesting thing to learn.
